### Problem: This Message Will Self-Destruct in 5s {#sec-cnt-pidx-message}

::: {.p-statement}
$N$ attendees are numbered $1 \ldots N$, and attendee $i$ has height $A_i$. Count the pairs $i < j$ whose numbers differ by exactly the sum of their heights: $j - i = A_i + A_j$.

Sample 1: $A = [2, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1]$ gives $3$ — the pairs $(1,4)$, $(2,6)$ and $(4,6)$ in 1-based numbering, e.g. $4 - 1 = 3 = 2 + 1$. Sample 2: $A = [5, 2, 4, 2, 8, 8]$ gives $0$. The third sample, $N = 32$, gives $22$.

Constraints: $2 \le N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, $1 \le A_i \le 10^9$.

Source: [AC abc166_e · This Message Will Self-Destruct in 5s](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc166/tasks/abc166_e){.solved}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The condition mixes **indices and values**, and the move is to separate them: put everything about $i$ on one side and everything about $j$ on the other. $j - i = A_i + A_j$ becomes $i + A_i = j - A_j$. Now the pair condition is "a key computed from the left member equals a key computed from the right member" — but the two keys are **different functions** ($i + A_i$ on the left, $j - A_j$ on the right), so a plain histogram with $\binom{c}{2}$ does not apply. Fix the right end instead (@sec-cnt-a3): sweep $j$, ask how many earlier $i$ had left-key $j - A_j$, then file $j$'s own left-key $j + A_j$. One map, one pass.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Test every pair.** $O(N^2)$ — $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ pairs at the limit, so only an oracle.
2. **Separate the indices, fix the right end.** Map from left-key $i + A_i$ to its count; for each $j$ add `cnt[j - A_j]` and then insert $j + A_j$. $O(N)$ expected time with a hash map.
3. **Drop impossible keys, use an array.** A right key $j - A_j$ is below $N$, and a left key $i + A_i$ above $N$ can never be matched — so ignore those and store the rest in an array of size $N + 1$. $O(N)$ worst case, no hashing.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Test every pair

::: {.form-next}
The statement with two loops, using 1-based numbers so the samples read as printed.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def msg_brute(A):
    n, ans = len(A), 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(i + 1, n + 1):
            if j - i == A[i - 1] + A[j - 1]:
                ans += 1
    return ans


MSG_S3 = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5, 8, 9, 7, 9, 3,
          2, 3, 8, 4, 6, 2, 6, 4, 3, 3, 8, 3, 2, 7, 9, 5]
assert msg_brute([2, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1]) == 3
assert msg_brute([5, 2, 4, 2, 8, 8]) == 0
assert msg_brute(MSG_S3) == 22
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int n;
    scanf("%d", &n);
    vector<long long> a(n + 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) scanf("%lld", &a[i]);
    long long ans = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j <= n; ++j)
            if (j - i == a[i] + a[j]) ++ans;
    printf("%lld\n", ans);
}
```
:::

#### Separate the indices, fix the right end

::: {.form-next}
Rewrite the condition as $i + A_i = j - A_j$. The left-key and right-key differ, so the sweep reads one key and writes the other: `ans += cnt[j - A_j]`, then `cnt[j + A_j] += 1`. $O(N)$ expected.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def msg_map(A):
    cnt, ans = {}, 0
    for j, h in enumerate(A, start=1):
        ans += cnt.get(j - h, 0)               # earlier i with i + A_i == j - A_j
        cnt[j + h] = cnt.get(j + h, 0) + 1     # j as a future left end
    return ans


assert msg_map([2, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1]) == 3
assert msg_map([5, 2, 4, 2, 8, 8]) == 0
assert msg_map(MSG_S3) == 22
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int n;
    scanf("%d", &n);
    unordered_map<long long, long long> cnt;
    long long ans = 0;
    for (long long j = 1; j <= n; ++j) {
        long long h;
        scanf("%lld", &h);
        auto it = cnt.find(j - h);
        if (it != cnt.end()) ans += it->second;
        ++cnt[j + h];
    }
    printf("%lld\n", ans);
}
```
:::

#### Drop impossible keys, use an array

::: {.form-next}
Every right key $j - A_j$ is at most $N - 1$, so a left key above $N$ is never asked for; and a right key below $1$ never finds anything. Keep only keys in $[1, N]$ and the map becomes an array indexed by key — the small-value trick of @sec-cnt-a5 applied to a computed key.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def msg_array(A):
    n = len(A)
    cnt = [0] * (n + 1)
    ans = 0
    for j, h in enumerate(A, start=1):
        if j - h >= 1:
            ans += cnt[j - h]
        if j + h <= n:                         # larger keys can never be matched
            cnt[j + h] += 1
    return ans


assert msg_array([2, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1]) == 3 and msg_array(MSG_S3) == 22
for _ in range(300):
    arr = [random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 14))]
    assert msg_array(arr) == msg_map(arr) == msg_brute(arr)
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int n;
    scanf("%d", &n);
    vector<long long> cnt(n + 1, 0);
    long long ans = 0;
    for (long long j = 1; j <= n; ++j) {
        long long h;
        scanf("%lld", &h);
        if (j - h >= 1) ans += cnt[j - h];
        if (j + h <= n) ++cnt[j + h];
    }
    printf("%lld\n", ans);
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Test every pair**: $O(N^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Separate the indices, fix the right end**: $O(N)$ expected time, $O(N)$ space. **Drop impossible keys, use an array**: $O(N)$ worst-case time, $O(N)$ space. The answer is at most $\binom{N}{2} \approx 2 \cdot 10^{10}$, and keys reach $2 \cdot 10^5 + 10^9$, so both need 64 bits in C++.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $A_i \ge 1$, so a pair with $j - i = 1$ needs $A_i + A_j = 1$, which is impossible: adjacent attendees never match.
- Equal keys for one index: $j - A_j = j + A_j$ would need $A_j = 0$, which the constraints rule out, so reading before writing is a habit here, not a necessity.
- Huge heights: $j + A_j > N$ for every $j$ — the answer is $0$ and form 3 never writes to the array.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Using one key for both sides.** Grouping by $i + A_i$ and adding $\binom{c}{2}$ counts pairs with $i + A_i = j + A_j$, a different condition.
- **Inserting before reading with the wrong key.** Read `cnt[j - A_j]` (the right-end key) and write `cnt[j + A_j]` (the left-end key); swapping them counts $j + A_j = i - A_i$, which has no solution with $i < j$.
- **Mixing 0-based and 1-based indices.** The keys shift by one on both sides if you are consistent; if you are not, sample 1 comes out wrong.
- **32-bit keys.** $j + A_j$ reaches $10^9 + 2 \cdot 10^5$, which fits in `int` only barely; the count needs `long long`.
:::

**Variants.** When the two keys are the same function the condition is symmetric and a histogram suffices — that is CF 1520D, $a_i - i = a_j - j$. @sec-cnt-pidx-pleasant mixes index and value through a *product*, which cannot be separated into two keys at all.

::: {.practice}
- [LC 2364 · Count Number of Bad Pairs](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-number-of-bad-pairs/){difficulty="Medium"} — the symmetric key $nums[i] - i$, then complementary counting: bad pairs are $\binom{n}{2}$ minus the good ones.
- [LC 1814 · Count Nice Pairs in an Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-nice-pairs-in-an-array/){difficulty="Medium"} — separate $nums[i] + rev(nums[j]) = nums[j] + rev(nums[i])$ into the key $nums[i] - rev(nums[i])$.
:::
